::: {.kw-overview}
Rejection dominates this issue, and the news is mostly about what does not work: a French multicentre randomised trial adding bortezomib to plasma exchange, immunoglobulin and corticosteroids for late antibody-mediated rejection found no efficacy signal and a near-doubling of serious adverse events, while a Berlin-led genotyping study of 165 biopsies argues that natural killer cell missing self does not itself generate microvascular inflammation but does make a donor-specific-antibody-positive biopsy more likely to show it. Against that therapeutic vacuum sits a practical review of HLA delisting — the strategy of selectively removing unacceptable antigens to get broadly sensitised candidates transplanted at all, a direct sequel to last week's French acceptable mismatch data, and a reminder that the field has no agreed immunological thresholds for doing it. A twenty-year Markov model written from the Italian health service perspective puts a number on the other half of the immunosuppression question, finding that belatacept's metabolic advantage over tacrolimus costs something close to €1.5 million per quality-adjusted life-year and has essentially no chance of being cost-effective at conventional willingness-to-pay thresholds. Donor utilisation and machine perfusion supply the issue's most operationally useful finding, an analysis of 3,502 donation-after-circulatory-death transplants in which the pump nearly halved the odds of delayed graft function after conventional procurement but added nothing at all after thoracoabdominal normothermic regional perfusion, alongside a Toronto series in which eight days of glecaprevir-pibrentasvir begun before implantation cleared hepatitis C in all 116 recipients of organs from viraemic donors. Two papers close the issue on the question of when, and from whom: pre-donation diabetes, though not impaired fasting glucose on its own, steepened the early fall in living donor kidney function across 771 donors, and a target trial emulation of 32,770 American recipients found that pre-emptive transplantation carries no survival advantage whatsoever — only less delayed graft function and better death-censored graft survival.
:::

### 1. [Bortezomib in combination with standard-of-care for late active antibody-mediated rejection with de novo donor-specific antibodies after kidney transplantation: a multicenter randomized trial](https://doi.org/10.3389/ti.2026.16702)
[Snanoudj R, Marquant F, Renaudin K, Dubois V, Koenig A, Arzouk N, Caillard S, Giral M, Jalal Eddine A, Mazouz H, Kamar N, Pernin V, Matignon M, Ouali N, Anglicheau D, Elie C. *Transpl Int*, 2026. PMID: 42846119.]{.kw-ref}

Late antibody-mediated rejection with de novo donor-specific antibodies has no treatment anyone can defend from randomised evidence, and proteasome inhibition — which kills the plasma cells making the antibody rather than mopping up the antibody itself — has been the most biologically plausible candidate for fifteen years. This French multicentre, open-label trial randomised 60 adult recipients between February 2015 and July 2019 to corticosteroids, plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin alone or with the same regimen plus two cycles of four bortezomib infusions; the median gap between transplantation and enrolment was 76 months in each arm, and rejection was subclinical in 60.0% and 66.7% respectively. The composite primary endpoint — a halving of immunodominant donor-specific antibody mean fluorescence intensity together with stable or improved microvascular inflammation and transplant glomerulopathy on a centrally read 12-month biopsy — was reached by 40.0% on bortezomib against 33.3% on standard care (risk ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 0.61 to 2.34, p = 0.59), and by 50.0% against 42.1% per protocol (risk ratio 1.19, 0.60 to 2.36, p = 0.62). Neither half of the composite moved: antibody fell by more than half in 56.7% against 46.7% (p = 0.44) and histology stabilised or improved in 56.7% of both arms (p = 1.00), with median immunodominant antibody reductions at 12 months of 60.2% and 60.0% — the sheer size of that fall in the control arm being the result most likely to change how a clinician reads any uncontrolled bortezomib series. Estimated glomerular filtration rate slopes were indistinguishable (−7.10 ± 2.19 against −4.68 ± 2.18 mL/min/1.73 m² per year, difference −2.42, −8.51 to 3.67), graft survival was 96.7% in both arms and nobody died, but serious adverse events hit 23 of 30 bortezomib patients (76.7%) against 14 of 30 (46.7%, p = 0.017), and 11 of the 30 could not complete both planned courses because of haematological, neurological or hepatic toxicity. The honest caveats are that recruitment closed at 60 of a planned 100 after a 30-month extension, leaving the trial underpowered against an optimistic assumed effect of 5% versus 25%; that randomisation left the bortezomib arm younger, more female and carrying more antibody; and that central reading found only 83.3% and 80.0% of the two arms actually met the microvascular inflammation threshold used locally to enrol them. A prespecified look at patients with baseline immunodominant antibody above 15,000 mean fluorescence intensity was the one place a signal appeared (42.1% against 8.3%, p = 0.10), which the authors rightly treat as a hypothesis rather than a subgroup to act on. For a UK unit the practical reading is that bortezomib should not be added to standard care for late antibody-mediated rejection outside a trial, and that the 60% antibody reduction seen on plasma exchange and immunoglobulin alone is the benchmark any future agent has to beat.

### 2. [NK cell missing self in microvascular inflammation with and without donor-specific antibodies](https://doi.org/10.1093/ndt/gfag231)
[Mordà B, Akifova A, Diebold M, Lachmann N, Pigorsch M, Vietzen H, Puchhammer-Stöckl E, Kühner LM, Berger SM, Lassahn A, Stauch D, Osmanodja B, Maggiore U, Böhmig GA, Budde K. *Nephrol Dial Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42841624.]{.kw-ref}

Last week's narrative review of donor-specific-antibody-negative microvascular inflammation named missing-self allorecognition as one of the candidate mechanisms converging on that histology; this study tests the hypothesis directly and largely declines to confirm it. The investigators took 165 kidney transplant biopsies and treated three diagnostic categories as competing events — microvascular inflammation with antibody (n = 91), microvascular inflammation without antibody (n = 35), and antibody without microvascular inflammation (n = 39) — then genotyped recipients and donors for killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors and HLA to establish missing self, defined as the absence of donor HLA ligands for the recipient's inhibitory receptors. They also tested whether four natural killer cell functional polymorphisms (FCGR3A V/F158, KLRK1 LNK/HNK, KLRC2 wild-type or deleted, and rs9916629) moderated any association, using cumulative incidence functions and cause-specific Cox models. Missing self was associated with a substantially lower hazard of landing in the antibody-positive, inflammation-free category (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% confidence interval 0.16 to 0.84, p = 0.017; adjusted hazard ratio 0.42, 0.18 to 1.00, p = 0.051), while the hypothesised excess of antibody-negative microvascular inflammation amounted only to a non-significant trend (hazard ratio 1.43, 0.71 to 2.89, p = 0.313; adjusted 1.53, 0.72 to 3.25, p = 0.269). None of the functional polymorphisms modified the relationship. The authors' own reading is the careful one: missing self does not appear to generate microvascular inflammation by itself, but in a recipient who has already made donor-specific antibody it makes a clean biopsy less likely — natural killer cells as an amplifier of antibody-driven injury rather than an independent cause of it. Two design limits keep this firmly exploratory and the paper says so: the cohort is biopsy-selected, so indication bias is unavoidable, and there is no fourth group of biopsies with neither antibody nor microvascular inflammation against which to anchor the comparisons. For UK practice there is nothing to do differently tomorrow, but the direction of travel matters for how a unit interprets a puzzling antibody-negative biopsy: the mechanism most often invoked to explain it is, on this evidence, not doing the explaining.

### 3. [Delisting Strategies in Highly Sensitised Kidney Transplant Candidates](https://doi.org/10.1093/ndt/gfag229)
[D'Angelo M, Zahradka I, Jaklova K, Maggiore U, Viklicky O. *Nephrol Dial Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42836549.]{.kw-ref}

Delisting is the quieter cousin of the acceptable mismatch programme covered in last week's issue: rather than allocating around a candidate's antibodies, the unacceptable antigen list is deliberately shortened, admitting incompatibilities judged less immunogenic or lower risk so that offers start arriving at all. This Prague-led practical review, written by a group running a national transplant centre, sets out what the approach involves and where the evidence stops. The recommended structure is stepwise — begin with the lowest-risk antibodies, and consider progressively higher-risk incompatibilities only as the realistic probability of any transplant recedes — which makes delisting a judgement about competing risks rather than a single immunological decision. The counterweight is stated plainly: transplanting across pre-existing donor-specific antibody still carries a higher rate of antibody-mediated rejection and worse graft outcomes, so the strategy depends on patient selection, multidisciplinary input and intensive post-transplant surveillance rather than on any protective effect of the delisting itself. The review's most useful observation for a national programme is how unstandardised the practice is: definitions, eligibility criteria and implementation differ substantially between centres and between countries, and there are no agreed immunological thresholds for which antibodies may be delisted at which strength, which leaves individual clinicians interpreting complex histocompatibility data at the point of an organ offer. No pooled estimates or effect sizes are presented — this is explicitly a synthesis of existing guidelines, published outcomes and desensitisation protocols assembled into decision support, not a meta-analysis. Read alongside the French registry data from last week, the pairing is instructive for UK readers: that paper showed what a formalised, nationally governed route for highly sensitised candidates can achieve without a graft survival penalty, and this one shows what the informal alternative looks like when each unit sets its own thresholds.

### 4. [Long-term cost-effectiveness of belatacept vs. tacrolimus in kidney transplantation: Trade-off between metabolic benefit and immunological risk](https://doi.org/10.1002/bcp.70859)
[Di Maria S, Puglia C, Provenzani A. *Br J Clin Pharmacol*, 2026. PMID: 42839365.]{.kw-ref}

Belatacept's case has always rested on avoiding what calcineurin inhibitors cost patients over decades — nephrotoxicity and new-onset diabetes after transplantation — which is an argument about the second and third decade of a graft, and therefore an argument a trial cannot settle. This analysis builds a five-state Markov cohort model over a 20-year horizon from the Italian National Health Service perspective (functioning graft, functioning graft with new-onset diabetes, graft loss, retransplantation, death), populated from comparative studies and a randomised trial, and complements it with individual-level Monte Carlo microsimulation to show the spread of trajectories rather than just the mean. Belatacept cost €340,569 per patient against €188,816 for tacrolimus, an incremental €151,753, and bought 11.19 quality-adjusted life-years against 11.10 — a gain of about 0.09, which produces an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €1,540,779 per quality-adjusted life-year and a negative incremental net monetary benefit at a €30,000 threshold. The scenario most generous to belatacept, assuming a genuine renal benefit, still left the ratio at €604,095 per quality-adjusted life-year, and probabilistic sensitivity analysis returned an aggregate €1,596,119 with approximately zero probability of cost-effectiveness anywhere between €30,000 and €50,000 per quality-adjusted life-year. The microsimulation did reproduce the clinical story that motivates belatacept — less new-onset diabetes, longer persistence of a functioning graft, with the quality-adjusted advantage appearing mainly in the second decade — so the finding is not that the drug does nothing but that the price asked for 0.09 quality-adjusted life-years is roughly fifty times what a European health system pays for anything else. The limitations are those of any model: the clinical inputs come from heterogeneous comparative studies rather than a single long-horizon trial, the cost structure is specific to the Italian health service, and a 20-year Markov horizon extrapolates well past the data. The authors are careful to leave one door open, noting that younger recipients or those at high metabolic risk might yet represent acceptable value but that establishing it would need a study built around age and metabolic-risk strata rather than assumption. For a UK commissioner the arithmetic transfers even if the euro figures do not, and the useful question it sharpens is not whether to fund belatacept broadly but which narrow group — a young recipient facing fifty years of exposure, or one who has already developed diabetes on tacrolimus — could plausibly clear a NICE threshold.

### 5. [Thoracoabdominal Normothermic Regional Perfusion Attenuates the Protective Effect of Hypothermic Machine Perfusion on Delayed Graft Function in DCD Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1155/joot/8082011)
[Asassfeh A, Kimura J, Luma E, Harris M, Arpali E, Dunn TB, Cooper M, Rawashdeh B. *J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42829574.]{.kw-ref}

Normothermic regional perfusion and the hypothermic pump both exist to undo ischaemic injury in donation after circulatory death kidneys, and both are now routinely applied to the same organ without anyone having asked whether the second adds anything to the first. This study takes the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network registry from January 2020 to December 2025, restricts it to 3,502 adult dialysis-dependent recipients of first deceased-donor kidney-only transplants, and splits them four ways by regional perfusion and by pump versus static cold storage: 1,433 and 381 in the conventional arm, 1,347 and 341 in the regional perfusion arm. Among conventionally procured kidneys the pump worked as expected, cutting delayed graft function from 53.8% to 44.2% (p = 0.0011) and remaining protective after adjustment for recipient age, sex and diabetes, kidney donor profile index and cold ischaemic time (adjusted odds ratio 0.56, 95% confidence interval 0.44 to 0.71). Among kidneys recovered with regional perfusion it did nothing at all — 26.7% against 27.0% unadjusted (p = 0.98), adjusted odds ratio 0.82 (0.62 to 1.08) — and the interaction term was formally significant (odds ratio 1.46, 1.02 to 2.09, p = 0.039). Regional perfusion without a pump reduced the odds of delayed graft function by around 70% against conventional procurement without one (adjusted odds ratio 0.30, 0.22 to 0.42), and the protective effect of the pump in the conventional arm held despite its being used preferentially on higher-risk organs with longer cold ischaemia (19.9 against 17.5 hours), which strengthens rather than weakens the result. Three-year death-censored graft survival was between 92.7% and 94.3% across all four groups with no difference whatever (log-rank p = 0.73), so the entire finding concerns early function and resource use rather than graft longevity. The decisive limitation is that the registry does not record regional perfusion at all: the authors infer it from donor heart disposition plus an agonal-to-clamp time of 40 minutes or more, excluding the ambiguous 31-to-39-minute band, and misclassification cannot be ruled out — nor were perfusion parameters, regional perfusion duration or any biochemical measure of organ quality available. With both technologies expanding in the UK and the pump carrying real cost and logistical burden, the implication a UK unit can act on is a question worth putting to its own data: if regional perfusion has already been performed, the case for pumping that kidney as well may need to be made rather than assumed.

### 6. [Short-course prophylaxis with the Toronto HCV protocol for recipients of non-liver solid organ transplants from donors with hepatitis C viraemia: a retrospective, matched cohort study](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-1253(26)00237-2)
[Aleyadeh W, Cypel M, Kim SJ, McDonald MA, Schiff J, Alba AC, Keshavjee S, Yacht K, Munyal D, Allan R, Wang J, Kumar D, Humar A, Feld JJ. *Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol*, 2026. PMID: 42810376.]{.kw-ref}

Accepting a kidney from a hepatitis C viraemic donor currently commits the recipient to an 8-to-12-week course of direct-acting antivirals after transplantation, with the cost, drug interactions and adherence problems that implies; this series asks whether eight days is enough. Toronto General Hospital treated 116 nucleic-acid-test-negative recipients of organs from 72 viraemic donors aged under 70 between February 2019 and December 2024 — 56 kidney (48%), 34 lung (29%), 16 heart (14%), six kidney-pancreas and four pancreas — with glecaprevir 300 mg, pibrentasvir 120 mg and ezetimibe 10 mg daily for eight days, the first dose given 6 to 12 hours before implantation and seven more afterwards, first as a pilot in 30 patients and then as institutional standard of care in 86. Every one of the 116 met the primary endpoint: 114 (98%) had undetectable hepatitis C RNA at 12 weeks and the two who died before that point were undetectable at their last measurement. Each kidney, lung and heart recipient was matched to up to four recipients of organs from non-viraemic donors on organ type, sex, age, transplant date and primary disease, giving 168 kidney controls; two-year overall survival among kidney recipients was 93.5% (95% confidence interval 81.1 to 97.9) against 94.8% (89.8 to 97.4) in controls (hazard ratio 1.50, 0.38 to 6.00, p = 0.57), and one-year estimated glomerular filtration rate was 63.9 mL/min/1.73 m² (SD 22.2) against 57.4 (20.9, p = 0.24). Across the 106 kidney, lung and heart recipients two-year survival was 83.9% (74.6 to 90.0) over a median 140 weeks of follow-up, with 25 deaths (22%) and no deaths among the pancreas or kidney-pancreas group. Safety was uneventful: nothing attributable to hepatitis C, no death, withdrawal or dose change attributed to the regimen, and no drug interaction of clinical consequence; the single adverse signal was a grade 3 alanine aminotransferase rise in one kidney recipient, whose liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis of no particular pattern, with steatosis but no fibrosis. The constraints are a single centre, a retrospective design, and a mixed-organ cohort in which kidney recipients are under half the total and the confidence intervals around organ-specific survival are correspondingly wide. For UK practice, where hepatitis C viraemic donors remain substantially underused and the length of post-transplant treatment is part of the reason, an eight-day regimen started the evening before implantation is the kind of logistical simplification that could change what a unit is willing to accept — subject to the prospective confirmation a single-centre series cannot provide.

### 7. [Post-Nephrectomy Renal Outcomes in Living Kidney Donors with Diabetes and Prediabetes: A Retrospective Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.1093/joneph/aajag254)
[Yin S, Zhou Y, Huang W, Huang X, Luo Y, Li X, Wu L, Song T, Lin T. *J Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42817833.]{.kw-ref}

Most living donor programmes exclude diabetes and accept impaired fasting glucose with unease, on a literature too thin to say whether either position is right. This cohort from West China Hospital followed 771 donors who underwent nephrectomy between 2017 and 2023 — 699 with normal glucose, 53 with impaired fasting glucose and 19 with diabetes — taking the acute slope of estimated glomerular filtration rate as the primary outcome, and paired the analysis with a targeted systematic review and meta-analysis of the existing evidence. Over a median 31 months no donor reached end-stage renal disease, which is the reassurance to lead with. Diabetic donors nonetheless fared measurably worse: 10.5% fell below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 45 mL/min/1.73 m² against 1.9% of those with impaired fasting glucose and 1.4% of normoglycaemic donors (p = 0.041), and their acute slope was steeper at −17.3 against −14.4 and −13.2 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (p = 0.038). On multivariable analysis diabetes remained independently associated with a steeper decline (β = −3.85, 95% confidence interval −7.24 to −0.47, p = 0.026) alongside microalbuminuria, hypertension and a raised body mass index — a cluster which suggests the relevant exposure is cardiometabolic burden rather than the glucose number in isolation. The finding most useful at an assessment clinic came from an exploratory subgroup: donors with impaired fasting glucose and a baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate below 90 mL/min/1.73 m² declined faster than those at or above 90 (p = 0.004), so impaired fasting glucose appears safe on its own but not when it arrives with reduced renal reserve. The accompanying meta-analysis pointed the same way, with worse renal function (p = 0.036) and more hypertension (p = 0.031) among dysglycaemic donors, though with high heterogeneity. The authors describe their own results as hypothesis-generating and the reasons are obvious — 19 diabetic and 53 impaired-fasting-glucose donors is a small base for an outcome measured in decades, and 31 months of follow-up cannot speak to lifetime risk. For a UK programme the usable rule of thumb is to stop treating impaired fasting glucose as a single binary and instead pair it with measured glomerular filtration rate, albuminuria and blood pressure before deciding.

### 8. [Survival Outcomes Following Preemptive vs Nonpreemptive Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.37964)
[Rampersad C, Liew IT, Liu K, Irish GL, Clayton PA, Knoll G, Naylor K, Kim SJ. *JAMA Netw Open*, 2026. PMID: 42848402.]{.kw-ref}

That transplanting before dialysis saves lives is one of the field's settled convictions, and it has always rested on comparisons vulnerable to exactly the biases that make pre-dialysis patients look healthier: confounding, selection, and the lead time a patient accrues simply by being transplanted earlier. This target trial emulation attacks all three. Using the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients from January 2005 to November 2023, the authors took 32,770 adult first kidney-alone recipients whose waiting time began at an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 20 mL/min/1.73 m² or below — 15,894 (48.5%) pre-emptive, mean age 53.7 years (SD 13.1), and 16,876 (51.5%) non-pre-emptive, mean age 54.5 (13.0) — balanced them with stabilised inverse probability of treatment weighting across confounders chosen from a directed acyclic graph, and fitted left-truncated Cox models specifically to remove lead-time bias, over more than 265,369 person-years in which 6,827 deaths occurred. Pre-emptive transplantation conferred no mortality benefit at all (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% confidence interval 0.96 to 1.07), with weighted survival curves separating by only about 1% to 2% a year. What it did deliver was better early graft behaviour: delayed graft function was substantially less likely (odds ratio 0.68, 0.64 to 0.72) and death-censored graft failure less frequent (hazard ratio 0.81, 0.74 to 0.88), though that second advantage largely disappeared once delayed graft function was adjusted for — which locates the mechanism squarely in avoided ischaemic injury rather than in any systemic benefit of having skipped dialysis. All-cause graft failure showed no difference (hazard ratio 0.96, 0.91 to 1.00). This remains an observational comparison of people who arrived at transplantation by different routes, and weighting cannot balance what the registry does not record, including the comorbidity and frailty that determine who gets transplanted pre-emptively in the first place; the authors make no causal claim. The implication for UK practice is a reframing rather than a reversal: pre-emptive transplantation is still worth organising, but the argument for it should be made in terms of avoiding delayed graft function and protecting the graft — which is also why it is the strategy to reach for when the offer is a marginal kidney — not in terms of a survival advantage these data do not support.
